title: Live-looking API secret hardcoded in source and exposed via a public endpoint
description: A secret-shaped constant (RAKUTEN_API_SECRET) is committed directly in app.js and is also returned verbatim in the JSON response of a public endpoint, exposing it to any client and to anyone with repository access.
root_cause: The secret is stored as a literal in source code instead of an environment variable or secret manager, and is additionally echoed back in an API response instead of being kept server-side only.
intended_behavior: The application should read the API secret from a runtime environment variable or secret store, use it only in server-to-server calls, and never include it in any response sent to a client.

trace.description: RAKUTEN_API_SECRET is defined as a plaintext string literal at module scope.
The constant is read inside a public route handler.
The secret value is included directly in the HTTP JSON response body sent to the client.

evidence.description: const RAKUTEN_API_SECRET = 'sk_live_51Hc9F3example_do_not_reuse'; -- committed as a plaintext literal.
res.json({ id: req.params.id, apiKeyUsed: RAKUTEN_API_SECRET }); -- the secret is echoed to the client.

conditions.description: No authentication required to reach the endpoint that leaks the secret.

execution.attacker_perspective: Any client calls the public endpoint and reads the secret straight out of the JSON response; anyone with read access to the repository (or its history) can also read it directly from source.
instructions: Send a GET request to /api/products/1/rakuten-link with no authentication.
Observe that the response body contains the full value of apiKeyUsed.
execution.observed_result: The response JSON includes the live secret value, and the same value is visible in plaintext in the repository source.

remediation.strategy: Move the secret to an environment variable (or a secret manager) loaded at runtime, remove it from source and git history, rotate the exposed key immediately, and stop returning it in any API response.

code_changes.fixed_code:
const RAKUTEN_API_SECRET = process.env.RAKUTEN_API_SECRET;
// ...and never include RAKUTEN_API_SECRET in a res.json(...) response.

likelihood.reason: The leaking endpoint is unauthenticated and the secret is also plainly visible in source/repository history.

impact.reason: A leaked live API key can be used by an attacker to impersonate the application against the third-party (Rakuten) API, potentially incurring cost or manipulating data under this account.

confidence.reason: The secret literal and its exposure point are both directly visible in a few lines of source with no ambiguity.

title: SQL injection in /api/products/search via unsanitized 'q' parameter
description: The product search endpoint builds a SQL query by directly concatenating the raw 'q' query-string parameter into a LIKE clause. Any client can inject arbitrary SQL, allowing data exfiltration (e.g. dumping unrelated tables) or database corruption.
root_cause: User-controlled input is interpolated into a SQL string with template literals instead of being passed as a bound parameter to sqlite3's parameterized query API.
intended_behavior: The endpoint should return products whose name contains the search keyword, using a parameterized query so the keyword is always treated as data, never as SQL syntax.

trace.description: req.query.q is read directly from the unauthenticated HTTP request with no validation or type check.
keyword is interpolated into the SQL string with a template literal, no escaping or parameter binding.
The unsanitized SQL string is executed directly against the sqlite3 database.

evidence.description: const sql = `SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%${keyword}%'`; -- keyword is attacker-controlled and unescaped.

conditions.description: No authentication required; the endpoint is publicly reachable.

execution.attacker_perspective: An anonymous client sends a crafted 'q' value that breaks out of the LIKE string and appends additional SQL.
payloads: GET /api/products/search?q=x%25' UNION SELECT username, password, 1 FROM users --
instructions: Send the payload above as the 'q' query parameter to /api/products/search.
Observe that the response includes rows from an unrelated table (e.g. 'users'), confirming the injected UNION SELECT executed.
execution.observed_result: The LIKE clause is broken out of and an attacker-supplied SELECT is appended and executed by the database driver, as shown by the string concatenation at the sink with no parameter binding.

remediation.strategy: Use sqlite3's parameterized query placeholders so user input is always bound as data, never concatenated into SQL text.

code_changes.fixed_code:
const sql = 'SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE ?';
db.all(sql, [`%${keyword}%`], (err, rows) => { ... });

likelihood.reason: The endpoint is unauthenticated and publicly reachable, and the injection point requires no special conditions to trigger.

impact.reason: Successful exploitation allows reading or corrupting arbitrary data in the database, including tables unrelated to products (e.g. user credentials).

confidence.reason: The vulnerable data flow from request parameter to raw SQL execution is fully visible in a single file with no intervening sanitization.
